clue.text: I can head out for estate

indicators.note: out here means put out of order, so the letters of the three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A command to leave the house and head for a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' looks like part of 'head out' (set off), but it is the anagram signal for I CAN HEAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A hacienda is a large landed estate or plantation in Spanish-speaking countries.

clue.text: Head of stable clipped tail

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter of stable is used

parts.note: clipped means cut, as hair or a hedge is cut

explanation.surface: The stable boss trimmed a horse's tail.
explanation.definitionFit: A scut is the short, upright tail of a rabbit, hare or deer.

clue.text: Instal one in a sumptuous abode

indicators.note: in tells us the word for one goes inside the word for instal

parts.note: to instal something is to place it
a means one, as in a single thing

explanation.surface: An instruction to move someone into a luxurious home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Instal one' reads as a single instruction, but it is two pieces: PLACE (instal) with A (one) put into it.
explanation.definitionFit: A palace is a grand residence, the very picture of a luxurious dwelling.

clue.text: Beast's nut or butt

parts.note: a hog is a beast, here in the possessive
nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: A pig's head can either be used for a nut or a headbutt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nut or butt' suggests a head-butt; in fact butt is a large cask.
explanation.definitionFit: A butt is a large barrel for wine or beer, and a hogshead is a large cask of similar kind.

clue.text: Where one might enjoy porridge that's healthy?

definitions.meaning: porridge is British slang for a prison sentence and nick is slang for a prison, so a pleasant jail would be a good nick
in fine physical condition, in good shape

explanation.surface: A question about where breakfast oats are best enjoyed.
explanation.walkthrough: In British slang 'porridge' is time served in prison and 'nick' is a prison; IN GOOD NICK is also a British idiom for in good condition.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom describes a person or thing in fine condition, which fits being healthy.

clue.text: Biddy introduced to one Greek goddess or another

indicators.note: introduced to means put into, so the word for biddy goes inside the goddess

parts.note: Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin
biddy and hen are both informal words for a woman

explanation.surface: A woman is presented to one Greek goddess after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'another' is the definition: having built ATE, one Greek goddess, the clue asks for another one.
explanation.definitionFit: Athene is the Greek goddess of wisdom, a second goddess beside Ate.

clue.text: Burglar on college building covers everything

parts.note: a cat burglar climbs into buildings, so a cat is a burglar
a hall is a large building

explanation.surface: A burglar climbing over a college building conceals everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Something all-embracing, meant to include every case, is described by this hyphenated term.

clue.text: Appetite overwhelms only child — a glutton

indicators.note: to overwhelm is to engulf, so the appetite word surrounds the child abbreviation

parts.note: lust is a strong appetite
OC is an abbreviation for only child

explanation.surface: A greedy appetite takes over a spoilt only child.
explanation.definitionFit: Locusts swarm and devour every crop, so the insect is a byword for a voracious eater.

clue.text: Fancy duck the navy consumed

parts.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so O
RN is the Royal Navy
consumed means ate

explanation.surface: Sailors ate a fancy duck dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Ornate means elaborately decorated, which is what fancy means as an adjective.

clue.text: Examine fellow found hiding in hold

indicators.note: hiding in means placed inside, so the fellow letter sits within the word for hold

parts.note: to sit can mean to hold a session, as a court sits

explanation.surface: Inspect the man discovered hiding in a ship's hold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hold' suggests a ship's cargo space, but it gives SIT, as a court sits or holds a session.
explanation.definitionFit: To sift is to scrutinise carefully, sorting the useful from the rest.

clue.text: Cat kept by defendant very much at home

indicators.note: kept by means held within, so the cat goes inside the word for defendant

parts.note: the accused is the defendant in a trial
a tom is a male cat

explanation.surface: A cat kept by someone on trial feels thoroughly at home.
explanation.definitionFit: To be used to something is to be comfortable and familiar with it, fully at ease.

clue.text: Cope with death on the river

parts.note: death is the end of life
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: Dealing with a death by the river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a river in North Yorkshire, England.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure is to bear or put up with a hardship, which is to cope with it.

clue.text: It's become posh in recent times to trap a boy, after all

parts.note: U means upper-class, posh

indicators.note: to trap is to hold inside, so the boy goes within the word for recent times

parts.note: lately means in recent times
Tim is a boy's name

explanation.surface: Lately it has become fashionable to snare a young man, after all.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases mean in the end, when everything has been taken into account.

clue.text: Doctor I sedated made stable

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A doctor confesses to sedating a patient to calm them down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor' reads as the speaker, but it is a verb meaning tamper with, signalling the anagram of I SEDATED.
explanation.definitionFit: To steady something is to make it firm and stable, here in the past tense.

clue.text: Articles mentioned originally in religious work

parts.note: an and the are the indefinite and definite articles

indicators.note: originally means at the start, so only the first letter of mentioned is taken

explanation.surface: Papers that first cited a piece of sacred writing.
explanation.definitionFit: An anthem is a choral composition set to a religious text, sung in church services.

clue.text: Request to dine in the lobby

indicators.note: in places the word for dine inside the word for lobby

parts.note: an entry is an entrance hall or lobby
to eat is to dine

explanation.surface: An invitation to eat in a hotel foyer.
explanation.definitionFit: An entreaty is an earnest plea or appeal, a request in the strongest sense.

clue.text: Think highly of poster on Slough

parts.note: an ad, short for advertisement, can be a poster
a slough is a bog or swamp, as is a mire

explanation.surface: Praise for a poster displayed in the English town of Slough.
explanation.walkthrough: Slough is a town west of London; here it is the noun meaning a swamp.
explanation.definitionFit: To admire is to regard with respect and approval, to esteem someone.

clue.text: See about flower in a wind

indicators.note: about means going round, so the cathedral city surrounds the flower

parts.note: a see is a bishop's diocese, and Ely is one in Cambridgeshire
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: Watching a flower blowing in the breeze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like a verb, but it is a bishop's see; the Isle of Ely in eastern England is a diocese.
explanation.definitionFit: An easterly is a wind blowing from the east.

clue.text: Quick and easy victory in gymnastics

indicators.note: in puts the victory word inside the gymnastics abbreviation

parts.note: PT is physical training, school gymnastics
a romp is a walkover, an easy win

explanation.surface: A fast, effortless win in a gymnastics competition.
explanation.definitionFit: Prompt means done without delay, fast and punctual.

clue.text: Advocate for energy restricted following test

indicators.note: following puts the energy and restricted letters after the test

parts.note: pro means for, in favour of
the MOT is the annual roadworthiness test for British cars
E is the symbol for energy in physics
R is the film rating for restricted

explanation.surface: A campaigner for limited energy use after an examination.
explanation.walkthrough: The MOT is Britain's yearly safety test for vehicles; 'following' puts E and R after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A promoter supports and champions a cause, as an advocate does.

clue.text: Scoundrel in opera scaled walls

indicators.note: walls means encloses, so the answer sits inside the run of letters of opera scaled

explanation.surface: A villain in an opera climbed over the walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'walls' looks like the object of 'scaled', but it is a verb: opera scaled walls in the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a dishonest or mischievous person, a rogue.

clue.text: Turkish spirit used to be smart

parts.note: raki is an aniseed spirit drunk in Turkey
SH is short for second-hand, which means used

explanation.surface: A Turkish drink once had a chic reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: SH, for second-hand, is a standard abbreviation in classified advertisements.
explanation.definitionFit: Rakish describes a dashing, jaunty style, a sense of smart as in stylish.

clue.text: Soldier advanced? Give in!

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, so a soldier
to advance money is to lend it, so lent

explanation.surface: A soldier moves forward and someone shouts at him to surrender.
explanation.definitionFit: To relent is to soften and yield, abandoning a hard stance.

clue.text: Earl in terrible hailstorm maintaining a temperature

indicators.note: in places the earl letter within the reworked storm
terrible suggests something wrecked, so the letters of hailstorm are mixed

explanation.surface: A nobleman caught in a fierce hailstorm keeps warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' makes ISOTHRMAL from HAILSTORM, and 'in' puts E (earl) into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Isothermal is a physics term for a process taking place at constant temperature.

clue.text: Egyptian in prison in France

definitions.note: a place in France rather than a phrase

indicators.note: in places the Egyptian abbreviation inside the prison word

parts.note: can is slang for prison
E is an abbreviation for Egyptian

explanation.surface: An Egyptian is locked up in a French jail.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a place found 'in France', a loose style this setter often uses.
explanation.definitionFit: Caen is a city in Normandy, so it is a place to be found within France.

clue.text: Nick is caught with a joint

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A man called Nick is arrested holding a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: A chip is a small notch or flaw, and so is a nick.

clue.text: Play in a small village

definitions.meaning: Shakespeare's tragedy of the Prince of Denmark
a little settlement, smaller than a village

explanation.surface: A drama staged in a small village.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both Shakespeare's Danish tragedy and a small rural settlement.

clue.text: Learner involved in awful beating — that's evident

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped up inside, so the learner letter goes in
awful suggests something mangled, so the letters of beating are rearranged

parts.note: L is for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A learner driver suffered a brutal beating, plain to see.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awful' makes TANGIBE from BEATING, and 'involved in' puts L (learner) into it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tangible means capable of being touched, hence real and clearly perceptible.
